title: Research Bite #41: Secondary School Mathematics Teachers' Accuracy at Predicting Student Errors
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #41 summarizes Aidan Stannard and Colin Foster's study of how accurately secondary mathematics teachers can predict student errors on diagnostic multiple-choice questions from Craig Barton's own Diagnostic Questions website. Seven teachers, with experience ranging from 3 to 40 years, took part in repeated short sessions predicting what percentage of students would choose each answer option before seeing the real large-scale data, with accuracy measured via Mean Absolute Percentage Point Error. Teachers were already good at identifying which misconception each distractor was designed to elicit, but their quantitative prediction accuracy improved rapidly and significantly with practice, with the sharpest gains occurring within the first three sessions. Critically, years of teaching experience had no association with either starting accuracy or the rate of improvement, suggesting this is a trainable skill rather than something that simply accrues with time in the classroom. Barton's classroom takeaway is that short, repeated, self-directed practice predicting diagnostic question responses is an accessible, low-cost form of professional development — though the small sample of seven teachers means the link between improved prediction and improved actual classroom teaching remains unconfirmed.
points: Teachers' accuracy at predicting the exact percentage of students choosing each answer option improved rapidly with repeated practice, with the steepest gains in the first three short sessions.

Years of teaching experience (ranging from 3 to 40 years in this sample) was not associated with either starting accuracy or the rate of improvement — this looks like a trainable skill, not one that simply accrues with tenure.
The professional development required is minimal: short, repeated sessions predicting responses to diagnostic multiple-choice questions, requiring no funding and little preparation.

The study cannot yet confirm that improved prediction accuracy translates into better real-classroom teaching or durable student learning gains — the seven-teacher sample limits how far the finding can be generalized.
quotes: The paper investigates how well mathematics teachers can anticipate the frequency of student mistakes on diagnostic multiple-choice questions.

Researchers found that while teachers were generally skilled at identifying the underlying errors and misconceptions the questions were designed to elicit, their prediction accuracy significantly improved over time with repeated practice.

Professional development focused on developing the ability to anticipate student errors (such as predicting responses to diagnostic questions) can lead to rapid and significant improvement in predictive accuracy.
This type of professional development is easy to conduct, requires little preparation, and a teacher could carry it out independently without needing external funding.
Teachers should exercise caution because the study had a small sample size (seven participants), limiting generalisation.

We conclude that professional development focused on developing teachers' ability to anticipate student errors could lead to rapid improvement in teachers' error prediction and be potentially valuable in improving their classroom teaching.
